nodes.text: telnet - this was mostly familiar as well, though the THM room did introduce one new thing: banner grabbing.

subNodes.text: basically since telnet is all cleartext and operates over TCP, you can use it to connect to any tcp port and see the server's raw response.
you connect to the service and read the initial response it sends back (the 'banner') which can have stuff like the name and version of the software running on that port.
since many services now require/enforce encryption, telnet may not for every situation. you can do this with curl and the openssl client too though, so it's ok
now that i think about it, maybe this is what nmap does
pretty cool. didn't know this was a thing

nodes.text: the final thing discussed in this room is netcat. i've used this before but I guess I just never really knew what it actually does / how it works?

subNodes.text: essentially it's like telnet except it also supports UDP, and it can also be a listener. makes sense.
so we can do banner grabbing with netcat too, in exactly the same way as with telnet. cool!

i've pretty much ONLY used netcat for reverse shells, but i never really knew how that worked. now i do - the victim machine opens one of these arbitrary network tunnels to our attacker machine (acting as a listener), and pipes the output of a process (e.g., /bin/bash) into that tunnel. whatever output that victim receives (i.e. whatever we as the attacker type in) gets piped into that process as input.
now that i know what's actually happening under the hood, this actually seems really simple now.

reflections: TL;DR: I finally know how a reverse shell ACTUALLY works. Netcat and telnet are cool.

nodes.text: TL;DR: the internet was built on cleartext protocols, but they're insecure, because anyone who has a network sniffer can see EVERYTHING. that was the main recurring takeaway from this room. The rest of it just explained how those protocols work - I finally learned how email works lol

The description of this room is "Learn about common protocols such as HTTP, FTP, POP3, SMTP and IMAP, along with related insecurities." I think I got the common protocols part down - just gotta brush up on the related insecurities bit. Let's go
Ok so most of this room was pretty simple

subNodes.text: Went over telnet, talked about how it's unsafe because it's a cleartext protocol
Went over HTTP, talked about how it's the backbone of the web, but is also a cleartext protocol
Went over FTP, how it's also insecure because it's a cleartext protocol
Need I say more?

nodes.text: The rest of the room was actually pretty helpful - i kinda forgot how email works.

subNodes.text: quick recap:
the email client sends the mail to a mail submission agent (MSA)
the MSA checks that mail for any errors or whatever and sends it to a mail transfer agent (MTA)
the mail is transfered across MTAs - this is basically the shipping/delivery part
the MTA delivers the mail to the recipient's mailbox - a mail delivery agent (MDA)
the recipient email client can then fetch the mail from that MDA
in other words, the delivery 'network' that the mail is transfered through is like a 'network' of MTAs; the MSA and MDA are what connect a sender and receiver to that 'network.'
in that chain of events:
SMTP sits between the sender's email client and the MSA
POP3 or IMAP sit between the MDA and the recipient email client
makes sense now. cool!

nodes.text: the thing with sending email is that SMTP can use cleartext - of course it can lmao, here we go again

subNodes.text: email spoofing is also possible. didn't know that was a thing. basically, SMTP itself doesn't validate the `mail from:` and `rcpt to:` fields; an attacker can manipulate the `mail from` to make it seem like the mail is coming from a legitimate address. interesting.

nodes.text: ah, sick - POP3 and IMAP can also use cleartext. so they're also insecure for the same reasons as pretty much every other cleartext protocol
i never understood why there were so many email protocols. SMTP makes sense now; that leaves IMAP and POP3. here's what I learned:

subNodes.text: both POP3 and IMAP are used for receiving mail; both do it in a different way. both have really fitting names.
POP3 is "Post Office Protocol v3:"
when a message is retrieved from the post office, the post office no longer has it. similarly, when a device retrieves a message from a POP3 server, the server deletes it
the client takes it out of the post office, and it's their responsibility now.
IMAP is "Internet Message Access Protocol:"
messages and their status, flags, folders, etc are all stored on that IMAP server, not in the email client
it's the "message access" server; messages are accessed on that server and don't leave the server.

reflections: TL;DR: the internet was built on cleartext protocols, but they're insecure, because anyone who has a network sniffer can see EVERYTHING. that was the main recurring takeaway from this room. The rest of it just explained how those protocols work - I finally learned how email works lol
